Show the math

    This is an estimate for planning. It covers federal income tax, FICA, and simplified state income tax. It does not include local or paid-leave taxes. Your employer's payroll system may calculate a different amount.

    Does the District of Columbia have an income tax?

    Yes, and the District collects it itself rather than through a state. Subsection 47-1806.03(a)(11) of the D.C. Code sets seven bands for tax years beginning after 2021: 4% on taxable income up to $10,000, then 6% to $40,000, 6.5% to $60,000, 8.5% to $250,000, 9.25% to $500,000, 9.75% to $1 million, and 10.75% above $1 million. The Office of Tax and Revenue prints the same table and treats you as taxable in the District if you were domiciled there at any point in the year or kept an abode there for 183 days or more.

    Two things make the District unlike a state of the same size. There is no county or city government underneath it, so the rate above is the entire local income tax and nothing else is withheld where you live. And the table is written once, for individuals, without a doubled version for couples: a joint return pushes the couple’s combined taxable income through the same dollar steps, so a married pair reaches the 8.5% band at the same $60,000 a single filer does. Spouses who file separate returns are each taxed as a single person under subsection (e).

    This page applies the seven published bands and subtracts a standard deduction, then stops: no DC credits, no itemised deductions, no additional Medicare surtax beyond the federal one. The 2026 data file behind the page carries a $16,100 deduction for a single filer, while § 47-1801.04 sets the basic standard deduction at $15,000 for 2025 and indexes it afterwards, so the model’s figure is in the same range but not the same number. Read the DC line as an estimate and use the D-40 instructions for the figure that goes on a return.

    How District of Columbia take-home pay is calculated

    1. Annualise the pay. Salary divided by the number of paydays in the frequency you chose, or an hourly rate times hours, with overtime paid at time and a half and folded into the same gross figure.
    2. Take out pre-tax benefits. Traditional 401(k) or 403(b) deferrals, HSA deposits, and Section 125 health premiums leave the wage base before either the District or the IRS charges income tax on it.
    3. Apply the District’s bands. The standard deduction comes off first, then 4% takes the first $10,000 of what remains, 6% the next $30,000, 6.5% the next $20,000, and 8.5% everything from $60,000 to $250,000. The 9.25%, 9.75%, and 10.75% bands only matter above those incomes.
    4. Apply the federal bands. The federal standard deduction for the filing status, then the marginal brackets, each charging only the slice of income that lands inside it.
    5. Add FICA. 6.2% for Social Security up to the annual wage base, 1.45% for Medicare on all wages, and the extra 0.9% Medicare rate once earnings pass the high-earner threshold.
    6. Subtract nothing for disability or leave. The District has no disability insurance payroll tax, and Universal Paid Leave is funded by an employer contribution of 0.75% of wages under § 32-541.03 rather than by withholding from the employee. Neither appears on a DC stub, and neither is subtracted here.

    The result is your net pay for the period you selected. Pay frequency matters: a biweekly schedule pays 26 times a year and a semi-monthly schedule 24, so the same salary produces different per-paycheck amounts.

    Worked example: $95,000 in District of Columbia

    A single filer earning $95,000 a year, paid bi-weekly in 2026:

    LinePer paycheck
    Gross pay$3,653.85
    Federal income tax$464.23
    Social Security$226.54
    Medicare$52.98
    District of Columbia state income tax$196.40
    Net take-home pay$2,713.69

    That is $70,556.00 a year, an effective tax rate of about 25.7%. Change the inputs in the calculator above to see your own numbers.

    How District of Columbia compares

    The District charges more than either neighbour at the top. Maryland’s state rate tops out at 5.75% and Virginia’s at 5.75%, and each adds a local layer — Maryland’s counties up to 3.2%, Virginia’s cities and counties up to 1%. Even the highest Maryland combination, 8.95%, is only about where DC already sits at $60,000 of taxable income, and the District’s 9.25% and 10.75% bands have no counterpart in either state. A DC salary and a suburban salary of the same size therefore do not net the same amount.

    Relief exists in one direction. A District resident who pays income tax to another jurisdiction on income taxed by both can claim a credit against the DC tax under § 47-1806.04(a), capped at the DC tax attributable to that income, and Virginia and Maryland extend credit or reciprocity in the other direction. What none of the three withholds is a disability premium, so the only local deduction on a DC stub is the income tax line itself.

    FAQ

    Does the District of Columbia have an income tax?

    Yes. D.C. Code § 47-1806.03(a)(11) taxes individual income in seven bands: 4% up to $10,000 of taxable income, 6% to $40,000, 6.5% to $60,000, 8.5% to $250,000, 9.25% to $500,000, 9.75% to $1 million, and 10.75% above $1 million. The Office of Tax and Revenue publishes the same schedule.

    How much is taken out of a $95,000 salary in the District of Columbia?

    For 2026, a single filer paid biweekly takes home about $2,713.69 per paycheck from a $95,000 salary: $3,653.85 gross, $464.23 federal income tax, $226.54 Social Security, $52.98 Medicare, and $196.40 DC income tax. That is $70,556.00 a year, an effective rate of about 25.7%.

    What is the top DC income tax rate?

    10.75%, charged on taxable income above $1 million. Below that the top bands are 9.75% from $500,000 to $1 million and 9.25% from $250,000 to $500,000. The 8.5% rate that most middle and upper-middle earners meet starts at $60,000 of taxable income for every filing status.

    Does DC withhold disability insurance or paid family leave from a paycheck?

    No. The District has no disability insurance payroll tax, and its Universal Paid Leave program is financed by a 0.75% contribution from covered employers under D.C. Code § 32-541.03, not by withholding from employees. This calculator subtracts no SDI and no paid leave premium, because a DC employee owes neither.

    Do DC's tax brackets double for a married couple?

    No. The District applies one rate table to a joint return's combined taxable income, so the $60,000 step into the 8.5% band falls at the same dollar amount for a couple as for a single filer. Two spouses living together who file separate returns are each treated as a single person under § 47-1806.03(e).

    What standard deduction does the District allow?

    Under § 47-1801.04 the basic standard deduction for 2025 is $15,000 for a single filer or a married person filing separately, $22,500 for a head of household, and $30,000 for a married couple filing jointly, with a cost-of-living adjustment for tax years beginning after 2025. The 2026 data used here applies $16,100 for a single filer, so this page's DC line runs slightly below a return claiming the statutory deduction.

    What form does a DC employee file for withholding?

    Form D-4, the Employee's District of Columbia Withholding Allowance Certificate, which the employee gives to the employer rather than to the Office of Tax and Revenue. A nonresident claiming exemption from DC withholding on wages files Form D-4A instead. Both are separate from the federal Form W-4.

    Is there a county or city income tax on top of the DC rate?

    No. The District government is the only local jurisdiction between the federal government and a DC address, so there is no county, city, or school-district income tax to add. Neighbouring Maryland and Virginia residents do face a local layer, which is one reason a DC stub and a suburban stub differ even at the same state rate.
